Simulate data from the ZISAR model

Source: R/simulate.R
rzisar.Rd

Draws one data set from the ZISAR model, on a regular lattice with queen contiguity (the Monte Carlo design of the ZISAR paper) or on a weights matrix supplied by the user. Covariates are independent standard normal; the first element of beta and of gamma is the intercept. With sigma0 > 0 the inflation predictor has a SAR field of its own (the general model of zisar()); the default sigma0 = 0 gives the restricted model.

Usage

rzisar(
  n_side,
  beta,
  rho,
  gamma,
  kappa = 2,
  sigma = 0.5,
  rho0 = 0,
  sigma0 = 0,
  W = NULL
)

Arguments

n_side

Side of the square lattice, so \(n\) = n_side^2 units. Ignored when W is supplied.

beta

Count-process coefficients, intercept first.

rho

Spatial autoregressive parameter, in \((-1, 1)\).

gamma

Zero-inflation coefficients, intercept first.

kappa

Negative binomial shape.

sigma

Standard deviation of the random effects.

rho0, sigma0

Spatial autoregressive parameter and standard deviation of the inflation field (general model). With sigma0 = 0 no field is drawn and the random-number stream is that of the restricted model.

W

Optional row-standardised weights matrix (or spdep listw) to use instead of the lattice.

Value

A list with

data

Data frame with the counts y, the count covariates x1, x2, ... and the inflation covariates z1, z2, ..., ready for zisar(y ~ x1 + ... | z1 + ..., data = data, W = W).

W

The weights matrix (sparse).

coords

Lattice coordinates (row, col), or NULL with a user-supplied W.

truth

The parameters used.

eta, g, mu, pi, s

Latent field, inflation field (zero in the restricted model), negative binomial means, inflation probabilities and structural-zero indicators.

Examples

set.seed(42)
sim <- rzisar(15, beta = c(1, 0.5, -0.3), rho = 0.5, gamma = c(-1, 0.7))
head(sim$data)
#>   y      x1      x2      z1
#> 1 6  1.3710 -0.1740 -1.3038
#> 2 0 -0.5647  0.5157 -0.2509
#> 3 0  0.3631 -0.2344  0.1710
#> 4 0  0.6329 -0.6585 -0.4035
#> 5 7  0.4043  1.2502  0.1047
#> 6 4 -0.1061 -0.2718 -0.3189
mean(sim$data$y == 0)
#> [1] 0.4622
